title: Swink Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Swink wells have a 40-foot median depth, but records range to 980 feet. See yields, water levels, permits and drilling costs.
h1: What Swink Well Records Tell a Rural Property Buyer
intro_html:
Swink sits on the plains in Otero County, where permitted wells are usually shallow but not always. Records within 5 miles include domestic, stock, irrigation and monitoring wells, with conditions that can change from one property to the next.

The most useful starting point is the nearby well record: depth, reported yield, static water level, aquifer and construction details. Use this page to understand the local pattern, then have a driller evaluate the specific lot before you buy or build.

sections.heading: Swink well depth: shallow plains wells with exceptions
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Swink is 40 feet, and the middle half runs from 32 to 60 feet. That points to shallow drilling in much of the local alluvial and plains-sediment setting. For a normal-looking lot, a drilling bid based on the median may be reasonable as a starting estimate, but it is not a guarantee.

The records also show a wide spread. Seventy-eight percent of wells are under 100 feet, while 10% are between 300 and 600 feet and 12% are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest recorded well is 980 feet. A driller should review nearby logs rather than price every Swink lot at 40 feet.

sections.heading: How much water a Swink well may produce
sections.html:
Reported well yields are strong overall, but the records are limited: only 114 wells report a pump yield. Among those, the median is 31.5 gallons per minute and the middle half ranges from 15.0 to 295.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-five percent report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Low-yield records are uncommon in this dataset. One percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and none report under 1 gallon per minute. That does not remove the risk of a poor new well. A test-pump result, storage tank and intended use matter, especially for irrigation or a larger household. Colorado exempt household-use wells also have a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Swink water levels and what the records can show
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 26 feet, with the middle half from 18 to 36 feet. In practical terms, many wells encounter a relatively shallow water level, but a static reading is not the same as a guaranteed pumping level. Water levels can change after pumping and can differ between nearby wells.

Only 19 wells report a static water level, so this is a limited local sample. The permit counts by decade do not provide a water-level trend: they show when permits were issued, not whether the water table is rising or falling. Ask for the original well construction report and a current measurement when evaluating a property.

sections.heading: Who drilled near Swink, and how old are the permits?
sections.html:
Swink has a long well history. The records include 91 permits from the 1950s, 64 from the 1960s, 47 from the 1970s, 53 from the 1980s, 141 from the 1990s, 159 from the 2000s, 47 from the 2010s and 33 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active drillers named in these records are Crandall, H A, with 87 wells; Hoffman, Earl, with 60; and Broce Drilling, Broce, Frank R., with 39. Those names help locate comparable logs, but an old nearby well is not proof of present performance. Confirm the current permit, use, construction and repair history through Colorado DWR before relying on it.

sections.heading: What a new well costs around Swink
sections.html:
Local ground conditions are described as alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. The drilling rate model is $35 to $55 per foot. At the 40-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $1,400 to $2,200.

That is only the hole. A finished well including the pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $7,400 to $14,200 at the median depth. A deeper-than-typical site can move well beyond that range, as can difficult access, casing, grout, additional trenching or an unexpected dry hole. Get a written bid that separates drilling from equipment and site work.

sections.heading: Swink risks: water quality, septic and building plans
sections.html:
The permit records name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer for 877 wells, the Dakota for 33 and the Cheyenne for 12. They show no Denver Basin aquifer wells. Fractured or variable formations can make results unpredictable, so do not assume a neighbor’s depth or yield will repeat on your lot.

Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 20 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 10 historic mine features and 15 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That is a reason to test the actual household water and investigate the property history, not proof that every well is contaminated. Check septic setbacks, soil, drainage, access for a rig, and the building location before finalizing a lot plan.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Swink: a practical check list
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit and construction record for the exact property. Then compare several nearby wells in Swink, La Junta Gardens, La Junta, Rocky Ford, North La Junta or Cheraw. Look for consistent depths, aquifer names, reported yields and static levels, while remembering that only a portion of records includes yield or water-level data.

For a purchase, make the well inspection and water test part of the contract process. For a new build, have a driller confirm access, target depth, casing and grout, pump sizing and storage before excavation begins. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, ask DWR or a water attorney whether an augmentation plan is needed for the proposed use. Plan septic and the home together so the well, drainfield and access routes fit the lot.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Swink, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth near Swink is 40 feet, and the middle half runs from 32 to 60 feet. Most records, 78%, are under 100 feet. The range is still wide: 12% are 600 feet or deeper, and the deepest recorded well is 980 feet. Nearby logs are more useful than the median alone for pricing a specific lot.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Swink?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $35 to $55 per foot. At the 40-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $1,400 to $2,200. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $7,400 to $14,200. Deeper drilling, difficult access, casing, grout or a dry hole can increase the final bill.

faq.q: How much water does a Swink well produce?
faq.a: Of the 114 Swink-area wells that report a pump yield, the median is 31.5 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 295.0 gallons per minute, and 75% report more than 15 gallons per minute. These figures do not guarantee a new well. Require a pump test and match the result to household, stock or irrigation needs.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Swink?
faq.a: The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 20 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 10 historic mine features and 15 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those listings do not establish the quality of a particular well. Test the property’s water before drinking it, including for concerns identified by the local health authority, and repeat testing when ownership or conditions change.

faq.q: Do Swink wells have enough water for a new home?
faq.a: Local records show a median reported yield of 31.5 gallons per minute, with no reported wells under 1 gallon per minute in the available yield data. However, only 114 wells report yield, and a new well can perform differently from its neighbors. Confirm the permitted use, pump-test result, storage needs and any augmentation requirement before building or buying.
